ACCMEPREI.name: Indicator 2.a - Percentage who would accept minority ethnic people as residents in their area; as a work colleague; as part of their family
ACCMEPREI.monitoring:
Monitoring from baseline (2014 - 2024)
Only comparisons of levels of acceptance of Eastern Europeans, Irish Travellers and Muslims between the baseline and current year is appropriate. Prior to 2017, instead of 'Other minority ethnic groups', this question asked about 'Chinese or Asian people'; and therefore, data from 2017 onwards is not directly comparable with previous years for this group.

For Eastern Europeans, Irish Travellers and Muslims, willingness to accept each as residents, as work colleagues, or as family members, increased significantly between 2014 and 2024. No significant changes were observed between 2023 and 2024.

DESTREI.name: Indicator 1.c - Percentage of students from minority ethnic communities who go on to Higher, Further Education, employment, unemployment, training compared with the general population
DESTREI.monitoring:
Monitoring from baseline (2013/14 - 2023/24)
At baseline, the biggest difference between white and minority ethnic school leavers was just under seven percentage points, when a lower proportion of minority ethnic school leavers went on to Further Education (white: 35.5%; minority ethnic: 28.6%). By 2023/24, the biggest difference, at 7 percentage points, was in school leavers going on to Higher Education; a higher proportion of minority ethnic school leavers went on to Higher Education compared with white school leavers (white: 39.9%; minority ethnic: 46.9%).

LEAVQUAREI.name: Indicator 1.a - Percentage (%) of children with 5 GCSEs with grades A*-C by ethnicity
LEAVQUAREI.monitoring:
Monitoring from baseline (2013/14 - 2023/24)
Compared with the baseline year (2013/14), by 2023/24 there has been an overall increase of 8.8 percentage points for white and 10.9 percentage points for minority ethnic young people leaving school with five or more GCSEs (Grade A* - C).
In 2023/24, there was a 1.1 percentage point difference between the two groups; at baseline there was a 3.2 percentage point difference, and the largest gap between the two groups was in 2019/20 (6.8 percentage point difference).

MEGPALREI.monitoring:
Monitoring from baseline (2014 - 2024)
In 2024, the percentage of people with friends from at least one minority ethnic community (58%) was significantly higher than the baseline position (2014: 42%). There was no significant change from the previous year (2023: 56%).

At baseline, respondents were most likely to have friends from the Polish (22%), Black (18%) and Chinese (16%) minority ethnic communities. In 2024, respondents were most likely to have friends from similar minority ethnic communities: Black (28%), Polish (26%), and South Asian (22%).

MEGPUBLIREI.name: Indicator 3.a - Percentage who think minority ethnic people participate ‘a little’ or ‘a lot’ in public life
MEGPUBLIREI.monitoring:
Monitoring from baseline (2014 – 2024)
The proportion of respondents who thought minority ethnic people participated ‘a little’ or ‘a lot’ in public life (i.e., in at least one of the roles presented) increased significantly in 2024 (76%) from both the baseline and the previous year (2014: 71%; 2023: 70%).

Considering the five roles individually, there were significant decreases in the proportions who thought minority ethnic people participated ‘a little’ or ‘a lot’ as media commentators, politicians, school governors and prominent business leaders between the baseline and the current year. There was a significant increase between the proportion who thought minority ethnic people participated ‘a little’ or ‘a lot’ as faith leaders from 2024 (61%) to the previous year (2023: 55%).

NOQUAREI.name: Indicator 1.b - Percentage (%) of pupils leaving school with no qualifications by ethnicity
NOQUAREI.monitoring:
Monitoring from baseline (2013/14 - 2023/24)
To consider these findings, and those of Indicator 1.c in context, it is important to be mindful that while the total number of white school leavers increased only slightly, from 22,171 in 2013/14 to 22,598 in 2023/24, the total number of minority ethnic school leavers more than doubled (from 465 to 1,143) over the same period.

In 2023/24, the proportion of white school leavers with no qualifications (0.9%) was slightly higher than the baseline (2013/14: 0.7%); the percentage of minority ethnic school leavers with no qualifications decreased from 5.8% to 1.7% over the same period.

Young people from minority ethnic groups represented 4.8% of all school leavers in 2023/24 but make up 8.3% of pupils leaving school with no qualifications, compared with 2.1% and 15.1% in 2013/14 respectively.
